message.content:
### Your Rights as a Tenant in Texas (as of 2026) Below is a concise overview of the key protections and obligations that apply to residential tenants in Texas. These rights are derived from state statutes (primarily the Texas Property Code), local ordinances, and general landlord‑tenant law. For specific situations—especially those involving disputes, evictions, or lease negotiations—consult a qualified attorney or your local tenant‑rights organization. | Area | What You’re Entitled To | Practical Tips | |------|------------------------|----------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlord may charge up to **one month’s rent** for a furnished unit and **two months’ rent** for an unfurnished unit.
• Must be returned within **30 days** after you move out, minus any lawful deductions. | Keep a written record of the deposit amount and any receipts. Ask for a written receipt when you pay. | | **Habitability** | • Landlord must keep the premises in a **safe, sanitary, and livable condition** (e.g., functioning plumbing, heating, electrical, pest control).
• Must repair or replace broken essential services within a reasonable time. | Document any problems (photos, written notices). If repairs are not made, you may withhold rent or pursue a “repair‑and‑deduct” remedy. | | **Rent Payment** | • Rent is due on the date specified in the lease. Late fees are allowed only if the lease states them and they are reasonable. | Keep copies of all rent payments (checks, bank statements). If you’re late, notify the landlord in writing. | | **Lease Terms** | • The lease must be in writing for any agreement lasting **more than one year**.
• The lease can’t contain illegal or unconscionable provisions. | Review the lease carefully before signing. Ask for clarification on any ambiguous clauses. | | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | • Landlord cannot enter your unit without **reasonable notice** (usually 24 hours) unless it’s an emergency. | If a landlord enters without notice, you can file a complaint or seek damages. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlord must provide a **written notice** (30 days for nonpayment, 60 days for lease violations, 90 days for no‑cause termination).
• Eviction can only proceed after a court order. | If you receive a notice, respond promptly. You may contest it in court. | | **Discrimination** | • Landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status, disability, or other protected classes (under the Fair Housing Act). | Keep records of any discriminatory actions. File a complaint with the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) or your state agency. | | **Privacy** | • Landlord must respect your privacy; they can’t monitor your activities or tamper with your personal belongings. | Report any unauthorized surveillance or tampering. | | **Maintenance of Common Areas** | • Landlord must keep common areas (hallways, stairwells, laundry rooms) clean and safe. | Notify the landlord in writing if common areas are unsafe. | | **Utilities** | • The lease should specify who pays utilities. If the landlord pays, they must maintain the service. | Verify utility responsibilities before signing. | | **Subletting & Assignment** | • You may sublet or assign the lease only with the landlord’s written consent (unless the lease allows it). | Get written permission and keep a copy. | | **Right to Repair and Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to repair a major defect, you may repair it yourself and deduct the cost from rent, provided you follow the proper procedure. | Keep receipts and give the landlord written notice before repairing. | | **Right to Withhold Rent** | • In certain circumstances (e.g., major habitability issues), you may legally withhold rent. | Consult an attorney before withholding rent. | | **Legal Remedies** | • You can sue for breach of contract, damages, or to enforce your rights. | Small claims court is available for disputes under $10,000. | | **Local Ordinances** | • Some cities (e.g., Austin, Dallas, Houston) have additional tenant protections, such as rent control, eviction moratoria, or mandatory mediation. | Check your city’s housing department for local rules. | --- #### Quick Checklist Before Signing a Lease 1. **Read the entire lease** – look for hidden fees, unreasonable clauses, or ambiguous language. 2. **Ask for a written receipt** for any security deposit or rent payment. 3. **Confirm the landlord’s responsibility** for utilities and maintenance. 4. **Verify the lease term** and notice requirements for termination. 5. **Check for local ordinances** that might affect your rights (e.g., rent control, eviction protections). --- #### When Things Go Wrong | Issue | First Step | Possible Remedy | |-------|------------|-----------------| | Landlord fails to repair a major defect | Send a written notice (email or certified mail) detailing the problem and requesting repair within a reasonable timeframe. | If no action, you may repair and deduct, or file a complaint with the Texas Attorney General’s Office. | | Unlawful eviction notice | Respond in writing, citing the proper notice period and your rights. | File a lawsuit in the county court to challenge the eviction. | | Discriminatory housing practices | Document the incident and file a complaint with HUD or the Texas Commission on Human Rights. | Seek damages and injunctive relief. | | Landlord enters without notice | Notify the landlord in writing that you are aware of the entry and that it was unlawful. | File a complaint with the local housing authority or pursue damages. | --- #### Resources - **Texas Attorney General – Consumer Protection Division**: [https://www.texasattorneygeneral.gov](https://www.texasattorneygeneral.gov) - **U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD)**: [https://www.hud.gov](https://www.hud.gov) - **Texas Commission on Human Rights**: [https://www.tchra.org](https://www.tchra.org) - **Local Tenant‑Rights Organizations** (e.g., Austin Tenants Union, Dallas Housing Coalition). - **Legal Aid Services**: Many counties offer free or low‑cost legal assistance for housing disputes. --- **Bottom line:** As a Texas tenant, you have the right to a safe, habitable home, fair treatment, and protection against unlawful eviction or discrimination. Keep thorough records, communicate in writing, and seek professional help if you encounter problems.
